concept.name: Monotonic Deque Techniques

relationships.description: Connects Monotonic Deque Techniques to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Maintain a double-ended queue in strictly increasing or decreasing order so sliding-window extrema and bounded DP transitions resolve in O(1) amortized time.
spark.keyTakeaway: Each index enters and leaves the deque at most once, turning O(N*K) scans and O(N log K) heap solutions into strictly O(N) single-pass algorithms.

concept.whyItMatters: Naive sliding-window maximum or minimum queries take O(N*K) time—timing out at 10^10 operations when N=10^6 and K=10^4—while balanced BSTs or lazy heaps add O(log K) overhead and memory bloat. A monotonic deque achieves exact O(N) time and O(K) space with minimal cache-friendly array operations.
whenToUse: Fixed or variable-width sliding window extrema queries (e.g., max CPU spike or min latency over the last K seconds).
Dynamic programming transitions of the form `dp[i] = opt_{i-K <= j < i}(dp[j]) + cost[i]`, reducing O(N*K) DP to O(N).
Subarray sum/difference constraints with negative numbers where a two-pointer window fails, such as shortest subarray with sum >= K via monotonic prefix sums.
whenNotToUse: Arbitrary range minimum/maximum queries (RMQ) with non-sliding random intervals—use a Sparse Table (O(1) query) or Segment Tree instead.
Window median or k-th order statistic queries, which require two heaps or an order-statistic tree rather than just extrema.
Streams requiring deletion of arbitrary middle elements rather than FIFO window expiration.
keyPoints: Store **indices** (not raw values) in the deque so you can evict expired elements from the front in O(1) via `dq[0] <= i - k`.
Before pushing `i` at the back, pop all indices `j` whose values are dominated by `nums[i]` (e.g., `nums[dq[-1]] <= nums[i]` for a sliding maximum).
Because dominated elements can never become the window maximum before `i` expires, popping them preserves correctness with zero information loss.
Amortized complexity is strictly O(N): every index is pushed once and popped at most once across the entire array.
For prefix-sum shortest-subarray problems (`P[i] - P[j] >= K`), maintain an increasing deque of prefix indices and pop from the front once `P[i] - P[dq[0]] >= K`.

examples.title: Sliding Window Maximum at N=1,000,000
examples.scenario: Computing the rolling 10,000-sample peak latency over 1M telemetry points in Python/Java.
examples.outcome: Brute force takes ~10^10 ops (TLE >10s) and a lazy max-heap takes ~2*10^7 ops (~450 ms); a monotonic decreasing deque executes <=2*10^6 operations and finishes in ~45 ms in Java `ArrayDeque`.

examples.title: O(N) Bounded-Jump DP Optimization (Jump Game VI)
examples.scenario: A robot collects scores along N=10^5 cells with max jump K=10^4, where `dp[i] = nums[i] + max(dp[i-K..i-1])`.
examples.outcome: Replacing the inner K-scan with a monotonic decreasing deque of `(dp[j], j)` cuts runtime from O(N*K) (~10^9 ops) to O(N) (~10^5 ops, <15 ms).

tradeOffs.pro: Strictly O(N) worst-case time and O(K) bounded memory, whereas a lazy heap can retain up to O(N) stale elements.
tradeOffs.con: Requires careful front-expiry and back-monotonicity invariants; heaps are slightly more forgiving for non-contiguous deletions.

tradeOffs.factor: Monotonic Deque vs. Segment Tree / Sparse Table
tradeOffs.pro: O(1) amortized per step and O(K) space with tiny constant factors.
tradeOffs.con: Only answers monotonic sliding-window queries; cannot answer arbitrary `[L, R]` range queries out of order.

tradeOffs.pro: Contiguous ring buffers (`ArrayDeque` in Java, `collections.deque` in CPython) maximize CPU L1 cache locality.
tradeOffs.con: Pointer-based `LinkedList` deques incur per-node heap allocations and GC pressure at 10^6+ elements.

failureModes.name: Storing Values Instead of Indices
failureModes.description: Pushing raw values prevents O(1) window-boundary expiration and breaks when duplicate values exist.
failureModes.mitigation: Always store integer indices in the deque and compare `nums[dq[-1]]` against `nums[i]`.

failureModes.name: Using `if` Instead of `while` on Back Eviction
failureModes.description: Popping only one element from the back violates the monotonic invariant and returns stale suboptimal answers.
failureModes.mitigation: Always use a `while` loop when popping dominated elements from the back (and when evicting expired elements if window jumps).

failureModes.name: Wrong Inequality Sign (`<` vs. `<=`)
failureModes.description: Keeping duplicate values unnecessarily or popping equal prefix sums prematurely can bloat space or miss shorter valid subarrays.
failureModes.mitigation: For sliding max, use `<=` on back-pop so the newest index survives longest; for `P[i] - P[j] >= K`, pop front while valid because any later `i'` gives a longer subarray.

failureModes.name: Reading Front Before First Full Window
failureModes.description: Recording `nums[dq[0]]` when `i < k - 1` emits partial-window outputs that shift the result array.
failureModes.mitigation: Guard output emission with `if i >= k - 1:` (for fixed window size `k`).

commonMistakes: Forgetting to evict `dq[0]` when `dq[0] <= i - k` before reading the window maximum.
Confusing monotonic stack (used for Next Greater Element) with monotonic deque (needed when the older front end must also expire).
Using `list.pop(0)` in Python (which is O(K) per pop, degrading the whole algorithm to O(N*K)) instead of `collections.deque.popleft()`.
Using `java.util.LinkedList` instead of `java.util.ArrayDeque` in performance-critical Java loops.
Applying sliding-window two-pointers to subarrays with negative numbers instead of monotonic deque over prefix sums.

sections.content:
## The idea

A **monotonic deque** is a double-ended queue whose elements remain strictly monotonic (either non-increasing for maxima or non-decreasing for minima) from front to back. Its power comes from **dominance pruning**: if index $a < b$ and $\text{val}[a] \le \text{val}[b]$, then $a$ expires earlier than $b$ *and* has a worse-or-equal value—so $a$ can never be the optimal answer in any future window containing $b$. By evicting dominated elements from the back and expired indices from the front, the front of the deque always holds the exact window optimum in $O(1)$ amortized time.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace **Sliding Window Maximum** on `nums = [1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7]` with `k = 3`:

1. `i=0 (val=1)`: Deque empty -> push `0`. `dq = [0]` (vals: `[1]`).
2. `i=1 (val=3)`: `nums[0]=1 <= 3`, pop `0` from back; push `1`. `dq = [1]` (vals: `[3]`).
3. `i=2 (val=-1)`: `3 > -1`, keep `1`; push `2`. `dq = [1, 2]` (vals: `[3, -1]`). Window full (`i >= 2`) -> emit `nums[1] = 3`.
4. `i=3 (val=-3)`: `-1 > -3`, push `3`. `dq = [1, 2, 3]`. Emit `nums[1] = 3`.
5. `i=4 (val=5)`: Front `1 <= 4 - 3` -> evict `1` from front. Back `3 (-3) <= 5` and `2 (-1) <= 5` -> pop both. Push `4`. `dq = [4]`. Emit `5`.
6. Continue through `i=7` -> outputs `[3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]` in 14 total push/pop operations.

sections.content:
## Amortized O(N) proof & key variants

Why is a `while` loop inside a `for` loop still $O(N)$? Define potential $\Phi = |\text{deque}|$. Each iteration executes 1 `append` ($+1$ op) and $m_i$ `pop`s. Because an index can only be popped if it was previously appended, $\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} m_i \le N$. Total deque mutations across all $N$ steps are bounded by $2N$.

- **Two-Deque Min/Max Window**: Maintain one increasing deque (min) and one decreasing deque (max) to track `max(window) - min(window) <= limit` in $O(N)$.
- **Prefix-Sum Shortest Subarray**: For arrays with negative values, build prefix sums `P` and maintain an increasing deque of indices. Once `P[i] - P[dq[0]] >= K`, `dq[0]` can be popped permanently because any future `j > i` would yield a strictly longer subarray.

## Sliding-window data structures compared

| Approach | Time Complexity | Space | Handles Arbitrary `[L, R]`? | Practical Runtime ($N=10^6, K=10^4$) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Brute Force Scan** | $O(N \cdot K)$ | $O(1)$ | Yes | ~10s+ (TLE) |
| **Lazy Max-Heap** | $O(N \log N)$ worst | $O(N)$ | No | ~350–500 ms |
| **Balanced BST / TreeMap** | $O(N \log K)$ | $O(K)$ | No | ~400–600 ms |
| **Monotonic Deque** | $O(N)$ amortized | $O(K)$ | No | ~35–55 ms (Java `ArrayDeque`) |

## Failure modes

Most monotonic deque bugs stem from **subtle boundary or data-structure choices**:

- **Python `list.pop(0)` Trap**: Using a dynamic array's `pop(0)` shifts $K$ elements on every expiry, silently turning $O(N)$ into $O(N \cdot K)$.
- **64-bit Prefix Overflow**: In Java/C++, prefix sums for `Shortest Subarray with Sum >= K` overflow 32-bit `int` when $N = 10^5$ and $|a_i| \le 10^5$ (max sum $10^{10}$).
- **Incorrect Dominance Direction**: Using `>=` vs `<=` backwards turns a sliding maximum into a sliding minimum.

## Production & implementation hardening

Write clean, bug-free implementations in Java and Python:

- **Java**: Use `Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>(k);` (or a primitive `int[k]` circular ring buffer for zero boxing overhead) and `long[] prefix` for prefix-sum variants.
- **Python**: Always use `from collections import deque` (`popleft()`, `pop()`, `append()`), which is implemented as a block-linked array in C with $O(1)$ ends.
- **Unit Test Edge Cases**: Always verify strictly increasing, strictly decreasing, all-equal, `k = 1`, and `k = N` inputs.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Store **indices** (not values) in the deque so front expiration is an exact `O(1)` comparison.
- [ ] Evict expired front indices (`dq[0] <= i - k`) before reading the optimum.
- [ ] Use a `while` loop on back-popping to maintain strict monotonicity.
- [ ] Guard output emission with `i >= k - 1` for fixed-size sliding windows.
- [ ] Use `collections.deque` (Python) or `ArrayDeque` / primitive ring buffer (Java) with `long` for prefix sums.

interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Monotonic Deque Techniques. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.

nodes.label: Front Expiry Guard
nodes.role: Pop front if dq[0] <= i - k

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Maintain a double-ended queue in strictly increasing or decreasing order so sliding-window extrema and bounded DP transitions resolve in O(1) amortized time.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Back Dominance Pruner applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Monotonic ArrayDeque.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Monotonic ArrayDeque experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Always store integer indices in the deque and compare `nums[dq[-1]]` against `nums[i]`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Each index enters and leaves the deque at most once, turning O(N*K) scans and O(N log K) heap solutions into strictly O(N) single-pass algorithms.
Avoid trap: Forgetting to evict `dq[0]` when `dq[0] <= i - k` before reading the window maximum.
Avoid trap: Confusing monotonic stack (used for Next Greater Element) with monotonic deque (needed when the older front end must also expire).
When to reach for it: Fixed or variable-width sliding window extrema queries (e.g., max CPU spike or min latency over the last K seconds).
When to reach for it: Dynamic programming transitions of the form `dp[i] = opt_{i-K <= j < i}(dp[j]) + cost[i]`, reducing O(N*K) DP to O(N).

putItTogether.title: Putting Monotonic Deque Techniques Together
putItTogether.summary: Each index enters and leaves the deque at most once, turning O(N*K) scans and O(N log K) heap solutions into strictly O(N) single-pass algorithms.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Monotonic Deque Techniques before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Brute force takes ~10^10 ops (TLE >10s) and a lazy max-heap takes ~2*10^7 ops (~450 ms); a monotonic decreasing deque executes <=2*10^6 operations and finishes in ~45 ms in Java `ArrayDeque`.
